heath_proof: Let a rational straight line A be set out, and three numbers E, BC, CD not having to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and further let CB also not have to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Let it be contrived that, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH. [X. 6] Now since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, therefore the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG. [X. 6] But the square on A is rational; therefore the square on FG is also rational; therefore FG is also rational. And, since E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, therefore neither has the square on A to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG. [X. 9] Again, since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH. [X. 6] But the square on FG is rational; therefore the square on GH is also rational; therefore GH is also rational. And, since BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on GH the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH. [X. 9] And both are rational; therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore FH is an apotome. [X. 73] I say next that it is also a sixth apotome. For since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH. [v. 22] But E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on A to the square on GH the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH; [X. 9] therefore neither of the straight lines FG, GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A. Now let the square on K be that by which the square on FG is greater than the square on GH. Since then, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as CB is to BD, so is the square on FG to the square on K. [v. 19] But CB has not to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with K. [X. 9] And the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K; therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG. And neither of the straight lines FG, GH is commensurable with the rational straight line A set out. Therefore FH is a sixth apotome. [X. Deff. III. 6] Therefore the sixth apotome FH has been found.

10.90
**Statement:** To find the sixth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let there be set out a rational straight line A, and let three numbers E, BC, and CD be given such that E does not have to BC, nor BC to CD, the ratio that a square number has to a square number. [This is possible since there are infinitely many such numbers.]

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG [by 10.6, since we can find FG such that this ratio holds]. Then the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [by 10.6]. Since E does not have to BC the ratio of a square number to a square number, the square on A does not have to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number, so A is incommensurable in length with FG [by 10.9]. Therefore FG is rational and incommensurable in length with A, so FG is irrational in the sense of being incommensurable in length with the assigned rational line A.

**Step 3.** Since BC does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [again by 10.6, finding GH accordingly], the square on FG is incommensurable with the square on GH [by 10.9]. Therefore FG is incommensurable in square with GH. Now both FG and GH are rational (commensurable in square with A), so FG and GH are rational and commensurable in square only. Therefore FH = FG - GH is an apotome [by 10.73].

**Step 4.** I say that FH is a sixth apotome. Since as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [by 5.22]. But E does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number (since E does not have to BC, nor BC to CD, the ratio of a square number to a square number, and neither does the product of such non-square ratios yield a square ratio). Therefore the square on A does not have to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number, so A is incommensurable in length with GH [by 10.9].

**Step 5.** Therefore neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A. This satisfies one condition for a sixth apotome [by D10.3.6].

**Step 6.** Now I must show that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG. Since as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore by conversion of ratio, as BC is to BD, so is the square on FG to the difference of the squares on FG and GH [by 5.19 with CN3], that is, to the square on the straight line K where the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 7.** We need BC not to have to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number. Since E, BC, CD were chosen so that BC does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, it follows that BC does not have to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number either [for if BC had to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number, then by 7.19 and the properties of numbers, BC would have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, contradicting our hypothesis].

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on FG does not have to the square on K the ratio of a square number to a square number, so FG is incommensurable in length with K [by 10.9]. Thus the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG.

**Step 9.** We have established: (i) FG and GH are rational and commensurable in square only, so FH is an apotome [by 10.73]; (ii) neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A; (iii) the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG. By definition D10.3.6, FH is a sixth apotome.

**Step 10.** Therefore the sixth apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.
